atomic_math_blocks.source_html: What to look for. (1) Gradient descent heads for $c$ and leaves $C$; projected gradient slides along the boundary to $x^\star$. (2) Beyond $\eta L=2$ the guarantee is gone: the steepest error component is multiplied by $|1-\eta L|\gt1$ per step, so gradient descent diverges from every start with such a component (almost every start), and at $\eta L=2$ that component flips sign forever without decaying. Larger $\kappa$ means zig-zags and more steps. (3) Penalty minimisers stay infeasible and the violation shrinks like $1/\rho$. The Hessian condition number usually grows with $\rho$, because the penalty adds curvature $\rho$ across the constraint only (half-space, disk, a single violated box bound); it does not when curvature is added in every direction: at a box corner with both upper bounds violated the Hessian is $Q+\rho I$ and the condition number falls towards $1$ (exactly $1$ for $\kappa=1$). (4) Barrier iterates never leave $C$, and at each centre $x^\star(t)$ the gap stays below $m/t$ (the readout compares the two at the last centre); from a start outside $C$ the barrier method cannot run.

flashcards.expected_result: $f(x')\ge f(x)-L\,d(x,x')$: with margin $s=f(x)-h\ge0$, every $x'$ within $s/L$ is certified (within $\omega^{-1}(s)$ for a modulus $\omega$).
assumptions: Assumptions of the linked section and conditions stated in answer.

flashcards.source_html: {q: 'Why does a grid check need the margin $Lr_c$?', a: 'Between nodes one only knows $f(x)\\ge f(g)-Lr_c$ ($r_c$ = covering radius), so $f(g)\\ge Lr_c$ at all nodes certifies $f\\ge0$ everywhere; $f(g)\\ge0$ does not.'
flashcards.theorem_statement: Why does a grid check need the margin $Lr_c$?
flashcards.expected_result: Between nodes one only knows $f(x)\ge f(g)-Lr_c$ ($r_c$ = covering radius), so $f(g)\ge Lr_c$ at all nodes certifies $f\ge0$ everywhere; $f(g)\ge0$ does not.
assumptions: Assumptions of the linked section and conditions stated in answer.

flashcards.source_html: {q: 'Three equivalent tests for convexity of a $C^2$ function?', a: 'Chords above the graph; tangent planes below it, $f(y)\\ge f(x)+\\nabla f(x)^{\\top}(y-x)$; $\\nabla^2f\\succeq0$ everywhere (a nonnegative diagonal is not enough).'
flashcards.theorem_statement: Three equivalent tests for convexity of a $C^2$ function?
flashcards.expected_result: Chords above the graph; tangent planes below it, $f(y)\ge f(x)+\nabla f(x)^{\top}(y-x)$; $\nabla^2f\succeq0$ everywhere (a nonnegative diagonal is not enough).
assumptions: Assumptions of the linked section and conditions stated in answer.

flashcards.source_html: {q: 'State Jensen\'s inequality in both directions.', a: 'Convex $f$: $f(\\mathbb EX)\\le\\mathbb Ef(X)$. Concave: reversed, e.g. $\\mathbb E\\sqrt X\\le\\sqrt{\\mathbb EX}$, $\\mathbb E\\log X\\le\\log\\mathbb EX$.'
flashcards.theorem_statement: State Jensen's inequality in both directions.
flashcards.expected_result: Convex $f$: $f(\mathbb EX)\le\mathbb Ef(X)$. Concave: reversed, e.g. $\mathbb E\sqrt X\le\sqrt{\mathbb EX}$, $\mathbb E\log X\le\log\mathbb EX$.
assumptions: Assumptions of the linked section and conditions stated in answer.

flashcards.source_html: {q: 'Define the convex conjugate and state Fenchel–Young.', a: '$f^*(y)=\\sup_x(y^{\\top}x-f(x))$, always convex; $f(x)+f^*(y)\\ge x^{\\top}y$, with equality iff $y\\in\\partial f(x)$.'
flashcards.theorem_statement: Define the convex conjugate and state Fenchel–Young.
flashcards.expected_result: $f^*(y)=\sup_x(y^{\top}x-f(x))$, always convex; $f(x)+f^*(y)\ge x^{\top}y$, with equality iff $y\in\partial f(x)$.
assumptions: Assumptions of the linked section and conditions stated in answer.

flashcards.source_html: {q: 'Gradient descent rates with $\\eta=1/L$?', a: 'Nonconvex: $\\min_{k\\lt K}\\|\\nabla f\\|^2\\le2L(f(x_0)-f_{\\inf})/K$. Convex: $f(x_K)-f^\\star\\le L\\|x_0-x^\\star\\|^2/(2K)$. Strongly convex: factor $(1-\\mu/L)^K$.'
flashcards.theorem_statement: Gradient descent rates with $\eta=1/L$?
flashcards.expected_result: Nonconvex: $\min_{k\lt K}\|\nabla f\|^2\le2L(f(x_0)-f_{\inf})/K$. Convex: $f(x_K)-f^\star\le L\|x_0-x^\star\|^2/(2K)$. Strongly convex: factor $(1-\mu/L)^K$.
assumptions: Assumptions of the linked section and conditions stated in answer.

flashcards.source_html: {q: 'Project $y$ onto $\\{a^{\\top}x\\le b\\}$ ($a\\ne0$) and onto a box.', a: '$y-\\frac{(a^{\\top}y-b)_+}{\\|a\\|^2}a$; clip each coordinate. The CBF-QP safety filter is such a projection.'
flashcards.theorem_statement: Project $y$ onto $\{a^{\top}x\le b\}$ ($a\ne0$) and onto a box.
flashcards.expected_result: $y-\frac{(a^{\top}y-b)_+}{\|a\|^2}a$; clip each coordinate. The CBF-QP safety filter is such a projection.
assumptions: Assumptions of the linked section and conditions stated in answer.

flashcards.source_html: {q: 'Penalty, slack, augmented Lagrangian, barrier: which give feasible answers?', a: 'Quadratic penalty, penalised slack: generally not for finite weights. Exact penalty: yes for a convex problem when the weight exceeds the optimal multiplier ($\\rho\\gt\\|\\lambda^\\star\\|_\\infty$, strong duality); nonconvex exactness needs more assumptions and may be only local. Augmented Lagrangian: in the limit, with finite $\\rho$. Barrier: steps that stay in the domain keep every iterate strictly feasible; only at an exact minimiser of $tf_0+\\phi$ is the convex gap $\\le m/t$ (approximate centring adds an error).'
flashcards.theorem_statement: Penalty, slack, augmented Lagrangian, barrier: which give feasible answers?
flashcards.expected_result: Quadratic penalty, penalised slack: generally not for finite weights. Exact penalty: yes for a convex problem when the weight exceeds the optimal multiplier ($\rho\gt\|\lambda^\star\|_\infty$, strong duality); nonconvex exactness needs more assumptions and may be only local. Augmented Lagrangian: in the limit, with finite $\rho$. Barrier: steps that stay in the domain keep every iterate strictly feasible; only at an exact minimiser of $tf_0+\phi$ is the convex gap $\le m/t$ (approximate centring adds an error).
assumptions: Assumptions of the linked section and conditions stated in answer.

flashcards.source_html: {q: '$\\sup$ vs $\\max$; what is $\\operatorname{arg\\,max}$; when does max-min equal min-max?', a: '$\\sup$ always exists in $[-\\infty,\\infty]$, $\\max$ only if attained; $\\operatorname{arg\\,max}$ is the set of maximisers (possibly empty or tied). $\\sup_y\\inf_xL\\le\\inf_x\\sup_yL$ always, with equality at a saddle point (convex-concave $L$ plus compactness).'
flashcards.theorem_statement: $\sup$ vs $\max$; what is $\operatorname{arg\,max}$; when does max-min equal min-max?
flashcards.expected_result: $\sup$ always exists in $[-\infty,\infty]$, $\max$ only if attained; $\operatorname{arg\,max}$ is the set of maximisers (possibly empty or tied). $\sup_y\inf_xL\le\inf_x\sup_yL$ always, with equality at a saddle point (convex-concave $L$ plus compactness).
assumptions: Assumptions of the linked section and conditions stated in answer.
